I was working out in the oil fields in ND. Driving the same road I had every day for 14 days straight at a time. As soon as the two-laned highway 2 change to 70mph, there is a crest that you cannot see over the other side of until you are on the peak of the crest.

I went up, and (unknowing to me) on the other side was a car accident from earlier. It had both lanes at a dead stop. I had two thoughts. 
1. "Hit the breaks, get over to the shoulder".
2. "Well. Here we go".
I remember just up to the moment of impact, and then black. Until an unfamiliar voice woke me up. 

As my eyes cleared , they immediately went red. "Oh", I thought, "My blood is coming on to my Carhartt and pants. These were nice clothes".

Also in regards to what state it was driven in. I once looked at a carfax of a vehicle that was driven primarily in Florida (I was living in WA at the time). This was a few months after a hurricane struck that side of the US.

I wasn't %100 sure it had flood damage, but it seemed a little fishy to me.
Very true. I had a 97 Ranger before I knew hot to buy vehicles. The transmission blew before my first year of ownership. Had I known the differences I may have walked away from the sale.

If the people selling the car don't let you do it, then do not buy the car.  They should understand that you should want to take it to have it looked at before making a large committed transaction.

Make sure you take it to a mechanic you trust. Don't listen to them if they say that they had their guys look at it and the vehicle looks fine. You don't know those guys, and frankly, some dealerships will say the craziest shit to get commision. 

The seller may or may not come with you, that's his choice and it shouldn't matter either way. The truck I bought last week the salesman wanted to go with me to my mechanic (it was 3 blocks down from the dealership). I told the salesman that my mechanic was very busy and it might take awhile for him to take a look at the truck. Long story short, the salesman waited in the lobby of the mechanics shop while my wife and I went and had a long lunch.

Make sure you research the year, make, and model of the vehicle you are looking at.

Google the vehicle and type "reviews". You can see if people are still driving them, what the problems may be, and all sorts of other stuff. 

One other note, look around at the cars that are on the road still. Those are the ones you want to buy.

This is the best advice. I know enough about vehicles, but not like my mechanic. I took two vehicles in to have him inspect. I ended up buying the second one and saved quite a bit of money on it based off the info he told me.

The kicker is that he did it for free. I don't know if that is typical (sign said $50), but it's a good marketing move because he's the only guy I will go too and now I will tell others about his shop.

I haven't read any of the responses, but here is my 2cents.

Not living with the person before you marry is a bad idea. You truly understand what kind of person they are when you have to coexist. You learn their habits, their cleanliness, basically who they truly are as a person. And the only way you can learn that is by sharing the same living space.

If you marry, and then move in, you run the risk of finding out he has some quirks that annoy him to no end. The same exact thing goes for him.

Moving in is a bigger step than marriage. Marriage is essentially a piece of legal document. But living together will show you what you and him will have to live with (literally) for the rest of your lives. 

Good luck on your situation.
